title: Backup and Production
subtitle: pg_dump, connection pooling, VACUUM, ANALYZE, and production configuration
author: KERNAL Team

content.code:
# Dump a database to SQL text file
pg_dump -h localhost -U postgres myapp > myapp_backup.sql

# Compressed backup (preferred for large databases)
pg_dump -h localhost -U postgres -F c myapp > myapp_backup.dump

# Restore from SQL file
psql -h localhost -U postgres -d myapp_restore < myapp_backup.sql

# Restore from compressed dump
pg_restore -h localhost -U postgres -d myapp_restore myapp_backup.dump

# Automated daily backups (crontab -e)
# 0 2 * * * pg_dump -U postgres myapp | gzip > /backups/myapp_$(date +\%Y\%m\%d).sql.gz

# Dump only the schema (no data)
pg_dump --schema-only -h localhost -U postgres myapp > schema.sql

# Dump only data (no schema)
pg_dump --data-only -h localhost -U postgres myapp > data.sql

-- VACUUM reclaims storage from dead rows (MVCC cleanup)
-- autovacuum runs this automatically — manual VACUUM rarely needed
VACUUM users;
VACUUM VERBOSE users;  -- shows statistics
VACUUM FULL users;     -- reclaims disk space (locks table — use sparingly)

-- ANALYZE updates query planner statistics
-- Run after bulk inserts/updates for accurate query plans
ANALYZE users;
ANALYZE;  -- analyze all tables

-- Check autovacuum status
SELECT
  schemaname,
  tablename,
  last_vacuum,
  last_autovacuum,
  last_analyze,
  n_dead_tup
FROM pg_stat_user_tables
ORDER BY n_dead_tup DESC;

items: Use a connection pooler — PgBouncer between your app and PostgreSQL. Each Postgres connection is a process (~5-10MB). 500 app connections → 500 Postgres processes without pooling.
Set max_connections — default 100. Increase to 200-400 with PgBouncer pooling. Formula: available RAM / 10MB per connection.
Enable pg_stat_statements — query performance tracking. Add to postgresql.conf: shared_preload_libraries = 'pg_stat_statements'
Configure shared_buffers — set to 25% of system RAM. The most impactful memory setting.
Regular backups — pg_dump or continuous WAL archiving (point-in-time recovery). Test restores regularly.
Use TIMESTAMPTZ everywhere — set timezone = 'UTC' in postgresql.conf so NOW() returns UTC.
Enable SSL — ssl = on in postgresql.conf. Require SSL in pg_hba.conf for remote connections.

questions.question: Your PostgreSQL server has 8GB of RAM and 200 application workers, each maintaining a persistent connection. Why is this a problem without connection pooling?
options: 200 Postgres processes × ~10MB each = 2GB used just for connection overhead, leaving less RAM for data caching
Only one connection can write at a time
pg_dump does not work with many connections
questions.explanation: Each PostgreSQL connection is a separate OS process, using ~5-10MB of memory for the connection itself (before any query work). 200 connections × 10MB = 2GB — 25% of your 8GB consumed just for connection overhead. A connection pooler (PgBouncer) multiplexes many app connections to a few actual Postgres connections, keeping connection overhead low.

faq.q: How often should I run pg_dump?
faq.a: For production: daily minimum, with automated rotation keeping 7-30 days of backups. Store backups off-server (S3, a different data center). For critical data, consider continuous WAL archiving (point-in-time recovery) so you can restore to any point in time, not just a daily snapshot.

examples: A startup lost months of user data because they had never tested restoring from their pg_dump backups — the dumps were running but the process was silently failing
PgBouncer is the standard production setup — Supabase, Railway, and most PaaS providers configure it automatically
